title: Moore, Escher, Penrose: A Conformal Golden Braid

paper.title: Moore, Escher, Penrose: A Conformal Golden Braid
paper.abstract:
Abstract “I don’t think I have ever done anything as peculiar in my life.
Among other things, it shows a young man looking with interest at a print
on the wall of an exhibition that features himself. How can this be?
Perhaps I am not far removed from Einstein’s curved universe.”
So wrote M. C. Escher about his 1956 lithograph Print Gallery .
Nearly half a century later, a mathematical analysis related its geometry
to an untwisted source image through a conformal power map z ↦ z α z\mapsto z^{\alpha} , α ∈ ℂ \alpha\in\mathbb{C} .
Building on this construction, we use a frozen text-to-image diffusion
model to generate new self-referential scenes.
Prompting alone does not enforce the recursion, while a post-hoc
transformation can leave structures poorly connected.
Applying the transformation during sampling is also insufficient:
the denoiser may “repair” the intended distortion or drift out
of the prescribed geometry.
We construct a generalized inverse T † T^{\dagger} of the non-invertible
image transformation T T , adapted to its recursive constraint.
In the idealized formulation, the Penrose identity T ​ T † ​ T = T TT^{\dagger}T=T makes T ​ T † TT^{\dagger} an idempotent projection onto geometrically
admissible images.
Yet denoising only the transformed image remains an out-of-distribution
task, even with projection.
We therefore braid denoising steps with T T and T † T^{\dagger} :
source-space steps develop the untwisted scene, while transformed-space
steps refine its appearance and connections in the final geometry.
We generate Print Gallery -like compositions and explore
further transformations.
Rather than distorting a finished image, we let the scene and its
distortion develop together. 1 1 1 The title echoes Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach: an Eternal Golden Braid ( Hofstadter, 1979 ) .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: “I went there expecting staircases coming out of the windows…” Roger Penrose, recalling his 1962 visit to M. C. Escher ( Wade, 2015 ) Maurits Cornelis Escher was not trained as a mathematician. Yet his art both inspired mathematicians and drew on their ideas. After encountering Escher’s work, Roger Penrose began devising impossible objects. The triangle and endless staircase he published with his father Lionel in 1958 subsequently inspired Escher’s Waterfall and Ascending and Descending ( Penrose and Penrose, 1958 ; Kersten, 2018 ; Kersten, 2019 ) . A different loop appears in the earlier Print Gallery (1956). A young man studies a print of a town; following its buildings brings us back to the gallery in which he stands. A picture contains the world that contains it ( Museum Escher in The Palace, n.d. ) . de Smit and Lenstra (2003) described the print’s idealized geometry through a conformal power map connecting a scale-periodic source to its transformed image. It specifies how coordinates correspond, not how buildings, objects, and textures should connect. We seek to generate scenes composed within this geometry, using a pretrained image model. Prompting for self-reference imposes no exact relation between image regions. Applying the transformation after generation enforces repetition, but leaves the model no opportunity to account for the resulting connections. Introducing it during sampling lets the model respond to the geometry, but subsequent denoising can alter corresponding regions independently or “repair” the intended distortion. Here, distortion is not a defect to remove, but part of the artistic intent. We use two coupled representations: an untwisted, scale-recursive source and its transformed image. A reverse coordinate warp alone is insufficient: the image transformation selects and repeats content, and a denoised image need not remain in its range. We therefore construct a matched generalized inverse T † T^{\dagger} that also acts on such images. Here Penrose returns through generalized inversion ( Moore, 1920 ; Penrose, 1955 ) . In the continuous construction, T ​ T † ​ T = T TT^{\dagger}T=T ensures that an admissible transformed image survives a round trip unchanged. Thus T ​ T † TT^{\dagger} is an idempotent projection onto the range of T T , restoring the constraint after updates, without a Euclidean nearest-point guarantee. Geometric consistency alone does not make a convincing composition. Denoising only the transformed image asks the model to interpret unfamiliar arrangements throughout generation. Braiding steps with T T and T † T^{\dagger} lets the same frozen model develop the source scene and its transformed appearance. For the Print Gallery construction, a zero-spin warm-up first encourages scale recursion. We contribute a matched generalized inverse and a braided sampler for recursive scene generation. The Penrose identities describe continuous operators; resampling and subsequent denoising introduce constraint error. sections.heading: 1.1 Related work
sections.text: “Originality is merely an illusion.” — M. C. Escher ( Locher, 1982 )

sections.heading: Escher’s geometry and computational art.
sections.text: de Smit and Lenstra (2003) formalized the geometry of Print Gallery and used it to reconstruct the missing central region. Cipolina-Kun et al. (2022) subsequently compared CoModGANs, LaMa, and GLIDE for completing the artwork: they straightened it into several views, inpainted these views, and transformed the completion back. Generation in the straightened representation is a direct precedent. We generate new scenes and repeatedly update both representations during sampling. Generative Escher Meshes ( Aigerman and Groueix, 2024 ) combines diffusion guidance with geometric constraints to synthesize tileable shapes and textures.

sections.heading: Self-similarity and generation across scales.
sections.text: Iterated function systems and fractal image coding represent structure through repeated contractive maps ( Hutchinson, 1981 ; Jacquin, 1992 ) . Neural Collages ( Poli et al., 2022 ) learns contractive operators whose fixed points represent images. Our geometry prescribes admissible images, with content from a frozen model. Generative Powers of Ten ( Wang et al., 2024 ) coordinates diffusion across scales for semantic zooms; ZoomLDM ( Yellapragada et al., 2025 ) learns generation at multiple magnifications. These methods allow content to change with scale, whereas our construction repeats the same content. Fractal Generative Models ( Li et al., 2025 ) uses architectural recursion without imposing this equality on outputs.

sections.heading: Constrained diffusion sampling.
sections.text: DDRM ( Kawar et al., 2022 ) exploits the spectral structure of linear inverse problems, while DDNM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) corrects clean-image estimates using a generalized inverse. DPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) uses approximate likelihood guidance for noisy linear and nonlinear measurements. Π \Pi GDM ( Song et al., 2023 ) also uses pseudoinverse-based guidance, including nonlinear and nondifferentiable measurement operators. Universal Guidance, Self-Guidance, and fast constrained sampling provide further ways to steer a frozen prior ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Epstein et al., 2023 ; Graikos et al., 2025 ) . Here the constraint relates regions of the generated image to one another, and sampling alternates between source and transformed representations using the matched operators.

sections.heading: Coupled views and geometric consistency.
sections.text: MultiDiffusion ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) fuses diffusion paths under shared constraints, and SyncTweedies ( Kim et al., 2024 ) synchronizes clean-image estimates through a canonical representation. Visual Anagrams ( Geng et al., 2024 ) combines denoising predictions under orthogonal image transformations. LookingGlass ( Chang et al., 2025 ) extends this approach to latent flow models and more general spatial warps through Laplacian-pyramid image processing. Diffusion Illusions ( Burgert et al., 2024 ) optimizes images whose arrangements reveal different interpretations. Tiled Diffusion ( Madar and Fried, 2025 ) enforces compatibility between tile boundaries, including self-tiling; Refracting Reality ( Yin et al., 2026 ) synchronizes directly and indirectly visible content using optical warps. These methods establish denoising across coupled views; our contribution is a matched operator pair for scale-recursive geometry and its use in sequential source/Escher sampling. The forward operator discards content outside a selected source band, while the generalized inverse selects its Droste extension. Their composition is an idempotent projector onto the twisted image class, allowing the constraint to be restored without compounding the warp. Braided sampling inserts source-space denoising between the inverse and forward maps to develop the scene within this recursive geometry.

sections.heading: Idempotence and generalized inversion.
sections.text: Idempotent Generative Network ( Shocher et al., 2024 ) trains a generator using an idempotence objective; here the geometric operator is specified analytically and the image prior is frozen. Gofer and Gilboa (2024) develop generalized inverses for nonlinear operators, including a norm-based pseudoinverse, while Ehrlich et al. (2026) construct surjective pseudo-invertible neural networks (SPNNs) and define inversion through a bijective completion. These formulations distinguish algebraic consistency from the criterion selecting an inverse.

sections.heading: 2.1 From scale repetition to Escher’s geometry
sections.text: The Droste effect is the repeated appearance of an image within itself. 2 2 2 The name comes from Droste cocoa packaging, which depicts a nurse carrying a tray with a smaller package bearing the same image. Following de Smit and Lenstra (2003) , we start with repetition under scaling alone, then apply a conformal power map to introduce rotation. Place the recursion centre at the origin and represent image locations by complex numbers z = x + i ​ y = r ​ e i ​ θ z=x+iy=re^{i\theta} . Denote this source class by 𝒮 \mathcal{S} .

Locally, away from the origin, this map is conformal : it preserves angles. Write log ⁡ z = log ⁡ r + i ​ θ \log z=\log r+i\theta . In these coordinates, scaling becomes a horizontal shift and rotation becomes a vertical shift. Multiplication by α \alpha rotates and scales this plane; exponentiation returns us to image coordinates.

sections.heading: Our inverse convention.
sections.text: We use T † T^{\dagger} to denote a chosen reflexive generalized inverse, selected by the scale-repeating Droste structure and matched fundamental bands. The dagger does not assert the Moore–Penrose minimum-norm or orthogonality properties. Its round trips restore recursive image structure; here, projection means idempotence, without a nearest-point claim.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We generate recursive scenes with a frozen text-to-image model by applying geometric maps to its predicted clean images between sampling steps. Alternating denoising with T T and its matched generalized inverse T † T^{\dagger} develops the untwisted scene and the connections created by its Escher transformation. Figure 3 shows this braided sampling process, from scale-repetition warm-up to final refinement in the transformed representation. Figure 3: Braided sampling. Warm-up interleaves denoising with untwisted repetition T 0 T_{0} . The sampler switches between Droste and Escher representations using T T and T † T^{\dagger} , with denoising blocks D ( n ) D^{(n)} between switches. It ends with refinement in the Escher representation. At each switch, 4 × 4\times super-resolution precedes the map, then resizing to working resolution. Dashed arrows indicate repetition; the noise-level axis is schematic. The early Droste preview is an illustrative blur of the later panel, not a recorded checkpoint.

T=E_{2}B_{1},\qquad T^{\dagger}=E_{1}B_{2}. (5) Each map keeps the selected band and regenerates the remaining image. This explains both its loss of information on arbitrary inputs and its ability to impose recursion in the destination representation.

Thus an admissible image survives a geometric round trip unchanged. For an arbitrary image, the round trip restores repetition from its selected band. On the admissible classes 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and ℰ \mathcal{E} , the maps are mutual inverses; on the ambient image spaces they are reflexive generalized inverses. The band boundaries and angular origin must agree between extraction and rendering.

sections.heading: Restoring the constraint without compounding the warp.
sections.text: Applying T T again to an Escher image generally compounds the coordinate warp; T T itself is not the projector onto the Escher class. The matched pair instead gives P ℰ = T ​ T † = E 2 ​ B 2 P_{\mathcal{E}}=TT^{\dagger}=E_{2}B_{2} , which is idempotent and fixes every admissible Escher image in the continuous construction. The inverse selects a Droste representative: it reads the chosen Escher band, untwists it, and extends it by scale repetition. Appendix C.1 gives an explicit construction. An immediate T † T^{\dagger} – T T round trip restores the constraint; our sampler additionally denoises in the Droste representation between these maps to update the scene content.

sections.text: The model can update a Droste image directly, or update its Escher rendering and carry the changes back: s → 𝑇 y → D ℰ y ~ → T † s ′ . s\xrightarrow{T}y\xrightarrow{D_{\mathcal{E}}}\widetilde{y}\xrightarrow{T^{\dagger}}s^{\prime}. Each geometric map ideally restores recursion in its destination, without an additional round-trip projection at the switch.

As an optional final step we re-noise the finished estimate to a moderate level ( σ tt = 0.75 \sigma_{\mathrm{tt}}=0.75 ) and denoise it once more without operators, so the prior can smooth the residual seams the warps may leave between repeated copies.

sections.heading: Varying the geometry.
sections.text: We explore five transformation families that arrange the scale-repeating source content in different geometries. For the conformal twist, β p = 1 − i ​ p ​ L / ( 2 ​ π ) \beta_{p}=1-ipL/(2\pi) advances p p source scale periods per output revolution; changing the sign of p p reverses the winding direction. Poles combines twists around several prescribed centres, while Möbius applies a Möbius coordinate change before the twist, producing two linked recursion centres. Square uses square-perimeter coordinates to produce square-shaped nesting, and Rimrings adds a radial term that packs repetitions near an outer circle. For Rimrings, we omit inverse steps because inversion is numerically unstable; visible divisions between repeated bands are intentional in this setting. Appendix C gives the map definitions and rendering details.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: The fixed recursion centre may miss the intended subject. In Figure 9 (left), warm-up anchors the nest on a window rather than the off-centre painter’s canvas. Optional time travel can also amplify seams instead of smoothing them, as the waterfall example shows (right pair). More generally, finite resolution and subsequent denoising limit geometric consistency: the continuous identities do not guarantee exact recursion in the final raster image.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Braided sampling combines a frozen image model with matched geometric maps to develop recursive scenes in source and transformed representations. Despite finite resolution and imperfect scene consistency, the results show how geometry can shape a composition throughout generation. “I never got a pass mark in math … mathematicians now use my prints to illustrate their books.” —M. C. Escher ( Ernst, 1976 )

sections.heading: B.1 Transfer to PixelDiT
sections.text: To test whether the recipe depends on latent-space denoising, we rerun it on PixelDiT-1300M ( nvidia/PixelDiT-1300M-1024px ), a 1.3 1.3 B-parameter pixel-space diffusion transformer with no VAE. It shares FLUX’s rectified-flow contract, so the operator step carries over unchanged, except that the VAE round trip becomes the identity and every T T and T † T^{\dagger} is a pure pixel-space warp of x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} . We keep the FLUX recipe above and match it step for step, changing only the noise schedule: at equal σ \sigma PixelDiT is further along, so FLUX’s values give hazy outputs. Re-matching the levels by correlating the running estimate with the final image (warm-up → 0.96 0.95\!\to\!0.96 , σ hi → 0.92 \sigma_{\mathrm{hi}}\,0.87\!\to\!0.92 , σ lo → 0.69 \sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}\,0.5\!\to\!0.69 , time travel → 0.82 0.75\!\to\!0.82 ) restores contrast and keeps the recursion. A 1024 2 1024^{2} image takes about 20 20 seconds on one RTX 5090 (versus ∼ \sim 2 minutes for FLUX). The resulting gallery is shown in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Appendix C Transformation definitions
sections.text: We use the source scale factor λ > 1 \lambda>1 and L = log ⁡ λ L=\log\lambda from Sec. 2.1 . After centering source coordinates, write the output-to-source sampling rule as y ⁡ ( w ) = s ⁡ ( exp ⁡ Q ⁡ ( w ) ) . y(w)=s\!\left(\exp Q(w)\right). Here Q Q is the source log-position, and a positive factor η \eta sets its overall image scale. Source scale repetition and angular periodicity identify log-positions that differ by an element of Λ = L ​ ℤ + 2 ​ π ​ i ​ ℤ . \Lambda=L\mathbb{Z}+2\pi i\mathbb{Z}. Consequently, a branch change that adds an element of Λ \Lambda does not change the sampled source colour. Define β k , l = l − i ​ k ​ L / ( 2 ​ π ) \beta_{k,l}=l-ikL/(2\pi) for integers k , l k,l .

sections.heading: Conformal twist.
sections.text: For integer p p we use Q ⁡ ( w ) = β p , 1 ​ log ⁡ w + log ⁡ η , β p , 1 = 1 − i ​ p ​ L 2 ​ π . Q(w)=\beta_{p,1}\log w+\log\eta,\qquad\beta_{p,1}=1-i\frac{pL}{2\pi}. A full turn changes Q Q by p ​ L + 2 ​ π ​ i ∈ Λ pL+2\pi i\in\Lambda . Thus p p counts signed source scale periods per output revolution. For w = r ​ e i ​ θ w=re^{i\theta} , a fixed source radius satisfies log ⁡ r + ( p ​ L / 2 ​ π ) ​ θ = const \log r+(pL/2\pi)\theta=\mathrm{const} , giving logarithmic spirals. Increasing | p | |p| changes their winding; the map is locally conformal away from the origin.

sections.heading: Poles.
sections.text: For prescribed centres c j c_{j} and integer pairs ( k j , l j ) (k_{j},l_{j}) , Q ⁡ ( w ) = ∑ j β k j , l j ​ log ⁡ ( w − c j ) + log ⁡ η . Q(w)=\sum_{j}\beta_{k_{j},l_{j}}\log(w-c_{j})+\log\eta. Each centre contributes a local recursion structure. A turn around c j c_{j} changes Q Q by k j ​ L + 2 ​ π ​ i ​ l j ∈ Λ k_{j}L+2\pi il_{j}\in\Lambda , so branch consistency holds separately at every centre. Away from the centres, the map is locally conformal wherever Q ′ ​ ( w ) = ∑ j β k j , l j / ( w − c j ) Q^{\prime}(w)=\sum_{j}\beta_{k_{j},l_{j}}/(w-c_{j}) is nonzero.

sections.heading: Möbius.
sections.text: For distinct points a , b a,b , we precompose the twist with M ⁡ ( w ) = ( w − a ) / ( w − b ) M(w)=(w-a)/(w-b) . The renderer uses Q ⁡ ( w ) = β k , l ​ [ log ⁡ ( w − a ) − log ⁡ ( w − b ) ] + log ⁡ η . Q(w)=\beta_{k,l}\bigl[\log(w-a)-\log(w-b)\bigr]+\log\eta. This is the two-centre case of Poles with opposite coefficients, linking the recursion around a a and b b . Different logarithm branches differ by source periods. This coordinate construction does not by itself specify a matched image-space inverse.

sections.heading: Square.
sections.text: For w = x + i ​ y w=x+iy , let ρ □ = max ⁡ ( | x | , | y | ) \rho_{\square}=\max(|x|,|y|) , and let τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \tau\in[0,1) be normalized arclength around the square perimeter, starting on the positive real axis. We use Q ⁡ ( w ) = l ​ log ⁡ ρ □ + k ​ L ​ τ + 2 ​ π ​ i ​ l ​ τ + log ⁡ η . Q(w)=l\log\rho_{\square}+kL\tau+2\pi il\tau+\log\eta. One perimeter traversal adds k ​ L + 2 ​ π ​ i ​ l ∈ Λ kL+2\pi il\in\Lambda . The square chart replaces circular nesting with square-shaped nesting. It is non-conformal, and its derivatives change across the rays through the square’s corners.

sections.heading: Rimrings.
sections.text: The ideal map adds a real radial term to the twist: Q ⁡ ( w ) = β k , l ​ log ⁡ w + h ⁡ ( | w | ) + log ⁡ η , h ⁡ ( r ) = A ​ r R 0 − r , A > 0 . Q(w)=\beta_{k,l}\log w+h(|w|)+\log\eta,\qquad h(r)=\frac{Ar}{R_{0}-r},\quad A>0. The radial term leaves angular branch consistency unchanged. As r → R 0 − r\to R_{0}^{-} , it traverses increasingly many source scale periods, crowding repeated bands near the outer circle. The implementation evaluates h h at min ⁡ ( | w | , R 0 − 10 − 3 ) \min(|w|,R_{0}-10^{-3}) to regularize the divergence. We do not apply an inverse for this transform: inversion is numerically unstable, and the visible divisions between bands are part of the desired appearance.

sections.heading: Rendering.
sections.text: All five maps specify output-to-source coordinates. Writing Q = u + i ​ θ Q=u+i\theta , the renderer chooses the largest-radius scale-equivalent sample that remains inside the source canvas. If r max ​ ( θ ) r_{\max}(\theta) is the available source radius in direction θ \theta , including a 0.995 0.995 safety factor, it uses m = ⌊ log ⁡ r max ​ ( θ ) − u L ⌋ , r src = exp ⁡ ( u + m ​ L ) . m=\left\lfloor\frac{\log r_{\max}(\theta)-u}{L}\right\rfloor,\qquad r_{\mathrm{src}}=\exp(u+mL). The standalone renderer samples these source positions bicubically on a supersampled output grid and averages to the final resolution. The in-loop implementation uses bilinear sampling (Table 2 ); the coordinate rules are shared. Replacing exact zero logarithm arguments by 10 − 9 10^{-9} avoids evaluating the logarithm at singular centres. The square radius is likewise floored at 10 − 9 10^{-9} . These formulas define the coordinate renderer; the matched-band inverse identities in Sec. 3.1 require the corresponding band extraction and extension construction.

Among other things, it shows a young man looking with interest at a print on the wall of an exhibition that features himself. How can this be? Perhaps I am not far removed from Einstein’s curved universe.” So wrote M. C. Escher about his 1956 lithograph Print Gallery . Nearly half a century later, a mathematical analysis related its geometry to an untwisted source image through a conformal power map z ↦ z α z\mapsto z^{\alpha} , α ∈ ℂ \alpha\in\mathbb{C} . Building on this construction, we use a frozen text-to-image diffusion model to generate new self-referential scenes. Prompting alone does not enforce the recursion, while a post-hoc transformation can leave structures poorly connected. Applying the transformation during sampling is also insufficient: the denoiser may “repair” the intended distortion or drift out of the prescribed geometry. We construct a generalized inverse T † T^{\dagger} of the non-invertible image transformation T T , adapted to its recursive constraint. In the idealized formulation, the Penrose identity T ​ T † ​ T = T TT^{\dagger}T=T makes T ​ T † TT^{\dagger} an idempotent projection onto geometrically admissible images. Yet denoising only the transformed image remains an out-of-distribution task, even with projection. We therefore braid denoising steps with T T and T † T^{\dagger} : source-space steps develop the untwisted scene, while transformed-space steps refine its appearance and connections in the final geometry. We generate Print Gallery -like compositions and explore further transformations. Rather than distorting a finished image, we let the scene and its distortion develop together. 1 1 1 The title echoes Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach: an Eternal Golden Braid ( Hofstadter, 1979 ) . See the animated supplementary material . 1 Introduction “I went there expecting staircases coming out of the windows…” Roger Penrose, recalling his 1962 visit to M. C. Escher ( Wade, 2015 ) Maurits Cornelis Escher was not trained as a mathematician. Yet his art both inspired mathematicians and drew on their ideas. After encountering Escher’s work, Roger Penrose began devising impossible objects. The triangle and endless staircase he published with his father Lionel in 1958 subsequently inspired Escher’s Waterfall and Ascending and Descending ( Penrose and Penrose, 1958 ; Kersten, 2018 ; Kersten, 2019 ) . A different loop appears in the earlier Print Gallery (1956). A young man studies a print of a town; following its buildings brings us back to the gallery in which he stands. A picture contains the world that contains it ( Museum Escher in The Palace, n.d. ) . de Smit and Lenstra (2003) described the print’s idealized geometry through a conformal power map connecting a scale-periodic source to its transformed image. It specifies how coordinates correspond, not how buildings, objects, and textures should connect. We seek to generate scenes composed within this geometry, using a pretrained image model. Prompting for self-reference imposes no exact relation between image regions. Applying the transformation after generation enforces repetition, but leaves the model no opportunity to account for the resulting connections. Introducing it during sampling lets the model respond to the geometry, but subsequent denoising can alter corresponding regions independently or “repair” the intended distortion. Here, distortion is not a defect to remove, but part of the artistic intent. We use two coupled representations: an untwisted, scale-recursive source and its transformed image. A reverse coordinate warp alone is insufficient: the image transformation selects and repeats content, and a denoised image need not remain in its range. We therefore construct a matched generalized inverse T † T^{\dagger} that also acts on such images. Here Penrose returns through generalized inversion ( Moore, 1920 ; Penrose, 1955 ) . In the continuous construction, T ​ T † ​ T = T TT^{\dagger}T=T ensures that an admissible transformed image survives a round trip unchanged. Thus T ​ T † TT^{\dagger} is an idempotent projection onto the range of T T , restoring the constraint after updates, without a Euclidean nearest-point guarantee. Geometric consistency alone does not make a convincing composition. Denoising only the transformed image asks the model to interpret unfamiliar arrangements throughout generation. Braiding steps with T T and T † T^{\dagger} lets the same frozen model develop the source scene and its transformed appearance. For the Print Gallery construction, a zero-spin warm-up first encourages scale recursion. We contribute a matched generalized inverse and a braided sampler for recursive scene generation. The Penrose identities describe continuous operators; resampling and subsequent denoising introduce constraint error. C. Escher ( Locher, 1982 ) Escher’s geometry and computational art. de Smit and Lenstra (2003) formalized the geometry of Print Gallery and used it to reconstruct the missing central region. Cipolina-Kun et al. (2022) subsequently compared CoModGANs, LaMa, and GLIDE for completing the artwork: they straightened it into several views, inpainted these views, and transformed the completion back. Generation in the straightened representation is a direct precedent. We generate new scenes and repeatedly update both representations during sampling. Generative Escher Meshes ( Aigerman and Groueix, 2024 ) combines diffusion guidance with geometric constraints to synthesize tileable shapes and textures. Self-similarity and generation across scales. Iterated function systems and fractal image coding represent structure through repeated contractive maps ( Hutchinson, 1981 ; Jacquin, 1992 ) . Neural Collages ( Poli et al., 2022 ) learns contractive operators whose fixed points represent images. Our geometry prescribes admissible images, with content from a frozen model. Generative Powers of Ten ( Wang et al., 2024 ) coordinates diffusion across scales for semantic zooms; ZoomLDM ( Yellapragada et al., 2025 ) learns generation at multiple magnifications. These methods allow content to change with scale, whereas our construction repeats the same content. Fractal Generative Models ( Li et al., 2025 ) uses architectural recursion without imposing this equality on outputs. Constrained diffusion sampling. DDRM ( Kawar et al., 2022 ) exploits the spectral structure of linear inverse problems, while DDNM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) corrects clean-image estimates using a generalized inverse. DPS ( Chung et al., 2023 ) uses approximate likelihood guidance for noisy linear and nonlinear measurements. Π \Pi GDM ( Song et al., 2023 ) also uses pseudoinverse-based guidance, including nonlinear and nondifferentiable measurement operators. Universal Guidance, Self-Guidance, and fast constrained sampling provide further ways to steer a frozen prior ( Bansal et al., 2023 ; Epstein et al., 2023 ; Graikos et al., 2025 ) . Here the constraint relates regions of the generated image to one another, and sampling alternates between source and transformed representations using the matched operators. Coupled views and geometric consistency. MultiDiffusion ( Bar-Tal et al., 2023 ) fuses diffusion paths under shared constraints, and SyncTweedies ( Kim et al., 2024 ) synchronizes clean-image estimates through a canonical representation. Visual Anagrams ( Geng et al., 2024 ) combines denoising predictions under orthogonal image transformations. LookingGlass ( Chang et al., 2025 ) extends this approach to latent flow models and more general spatial warps through Laplacian-pyramid image processing. Diffusion Illusions ( Burgert et al., 2024 ) optimizes images whose arrangements reveal different interpretations. Tiled Diffusion ( Madar and Fried, 2025 ) enforces compatibility between tile boundaries, including self-tiling; Refracting Reality ( Yin et al., 2026 ) synchronizes directly and indirectly visible content using optical warps. These methods establish denoising across coupled views; our contribution is a matched operator pair for scale-recursive geometry and its use in sequential source/Escher sampling. The forward operator discards content outside a selected source band, while the generalized inverse selects its Droste extension. Their composition is an idempotent projector onto the twisted image class, allowing the constraint to be restored without compounding the warp. Braided sampling inserts source-space denoising between the inverse and forward maps to develop the scene within this recursive geometry. Idempotence and generalized inversion. Idempotent Generative Network ( Shocher et al., 2024 ) trains a generator using an idempotence objective; here the geometric operator is specified analytically and the image prior is frozen. Gofer and Gilboa (2024) develop generalized inverses for nonlinear operators, including a norm-based pseudoinverse, while Ehrlich et al. (2026) construct surjective pseudo-invertible neural networks (SPNNs) and define inversion through a bijective completion. These formulations distinguish algebraic consistency from the criterion selecting an inverse. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 From scale repetition to Escher’s geometry The Droste effect is the repeated appearance of an image within itself. 2 2 2 The name comes from Droste cocoa packaging, which depicts a nurse carrying a tray with a smaller package bearing the same image. Varying the geometry. We explore five transformation families that arrange the scale-repeating source content in different geometries. For the conformal twist, β p = 1 − i ​ p ​ L / ( 2 ​ π ) \beta_{p}=1-ipL/(2\pi) advances p p source scale periods per output revolution; changing the sign of p p reverses the winding direction. Poles combines twists around several prescribed centres, while Möbius applies a Möbius coordinate change before the twist, producing two linked recursion centres. Square uses square-perimeter coordinates to produce square-shaped nesting, and Rimrings adds a radial term that packs repetitions near an outer circle. For Rimrings, we omit inverse steps because inversion is numerically unstable; visible divisions between repeated bands are intentional in this setting. In Figure 9 (left), warm-up anchors the nest on a window rather than the off-centre painter’s canvas. Optional time travel can also amplify seams instead of smoothing them, as the waterfall example shows (right pair). More generally, finite resolution and subsequent denoising limit geometric consistency: the continuous identities do not guarantee exact recursion in the final raster image. 6 Conclusion Braided sampling combines a frozen image model with matched geometric maps to develop recursive scenes in source and transformed representations.
